\title{Testing Digital Signal Processing Code\\without an Oracle: Metamorphic Relations,\\Domain Generators and Error-Model Tolerances}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Cl\'ement Basdevant}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Independent Researcher\\
ORCID 0009-0004-7496-2365}
\and
\IEEEauthorblockN{Nicolas Boganski}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textcolor{red}{[Affiliation to be completed]}}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Signal processing code is hard to test because the correct output of a filter,
a transform or a resampler on an arbitrary input is unknown. Libraries therefore
compare a few hand-picked cases with values computed by another tool, under
tolerances chosen by hand: in the test suite of \code{scipy.signal} alone we count
\surveyScipyDistinctTol{} distinct hand-written tolerances spanning
\surveyScipyTolDecades{} orders of magnitude, and no test in the five suites we
surveyed generates its inputs. We present dsp-props, an open-source Python
library that tests signal processing operators against properties every correct
implementation must satisfy (linearity, shift and convolution theorems,
Parseval's identity, causality, consistency with a declared transfer function,
periodic time invariance of resamplers, invariance of streaming processors to
block boundaries), on inputs drawn from signal families known to break such code,
with tolerances derived from an error model of each operation rather than chosen
by hand. On \nMutAuto{} automatically generated faults in four reference
implementations, dsp-props detects \killFuncDsp{} of the non-equivalent faults
and test suites ported from NumPy and SciPy detect \killFuncSop{}; the two miss
different faults and together detect all of them. On \nMutHand{} hand-written
faults, every variant detects every fault, and ablations show that the domain
generators and the error-model tolerances make failures appear sooner, with
smaller counterexamples, and without false alarms on subnormal inputs.
On correct implementations it raised no false alarm in \fpRuns{} runs. Applied to SciPy,
NumPy, PyTorch, librosa and torchaudio, it found faults that were reported upstream.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
software testing, metamorphic testing, property-based testing, digital signal processing, floating-point error, test oracle
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% ===========================================================================

Digital signal processing (DSP) code sits at the bottom of a large software
stack: the fast Fourier transform (FFT), linear filters and sample-rate
converters of NumPy~\cite{harris2020numpy}, SciPy~\cite{virtanen2020scipy} and
PyTorch~\cite{paszke2019pytorch} are called by audio, communication,
geophysics and machine-learning code that rarely re-checks them. Testing these
operators faces three problems at once.

\paragraph*{P1, no oracle} For most inputs nobody knows the exact output of a
filter or a transform. This is the \emph{oracle problem} of software
testing~\cite{barr2015oracle}, and it is acute for scientific
software~\cite{kanewala2014scientific}. In practice, tests compare against
values computed by another tool and typed into the test file, or against a
second implementation that may share the same assumptions. In the suites we
surveyed (Section~\ref{sec:survey}), \surveyScipyHardcoded{} tests of
\code{scipy.signal} compare with hard-coded arrays.

\paragraph*{P2, inputs that do not exercise the faults} Hand-written tests use
a few lengths and smooth or random signals. Faults in DSP code, however, hide in
specific places: lengths that are prime, odd or one away from a power of two
(which change the FFT algorithm), tones between two DFT bins or close to the
Nyquist frequency, extreme amplitudes, and, for streaming code, empty or
one-sample blocks. A concrete case: \code{scipy.signal.lfilter} returned an
uninitialised final state when given an empty block and an initial state
(SciPy issue gh-22571), so that any block-processing loop silently diverged
after an empty block; \code{sosfilt} still raises on such input. Across the
\surveyTotalTests{} tests we surveyed, only \surveyZiEmpty{} combine an initial
state with an empty input, and none generates its inputs.

\paragraph*{P3, no principled tolerance} Even when the expected output is
known, floating-point results are only close to it, and \emph{how close} depends
on the operation, the length and the conditioning of the problem. Tests
therefore use tolerances chosen by hand: \surveyScipyDistinctTol{} distinct
values in \code{scipy.signal}, from \surveyScipyTolMin{} to \surveyScipyTolMax.
A tolerance that is too loose hides a single-precision intermediate; one that is
too tight produces false alarms, which teach maintainers to loosen tolerances
further.

Property-based testing~\cite{claessen2000quickcheck,maciver2019hypothesis}
answers P2 in general by generating inputs, and metamorphic
testing~\cite{chen2018metamorphic,segura2016metamorphic} answers P1 in general
by checking relations between outputs instead of the outputs themselves.
Neither tells a DSP developer which relations hold for which operator, which
signals to generate, nor how to compare floating-point results; and a test tool
that claims to find faults in numerical libraries must itself be shown not to
raise false alarms.

This article makes the following contributions.
\begin{itemize}
\item A catalogue of metamorphic relations for four classes of DSP operators
(transforms, linear time-invariant filters, rational resamplers, streaming
processors), each with a proof (Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}), selected by a
one-line declaration of what the operator is (answers P1).
\item Signal generators that target the inputs known to break DSP code (P2).
\item Tolerances derived from forward error bounds of the FFT and of linear
recursions, and a calibration procedure that measures an implementation against
an extended-precision reference but refuses to absorb an implausibly large error
(P3).
\item An evaluation protocol that compares the approach with the test suites of
NumPy and SciPy on automatically generated faults, isolates the contribution of
the generators and of the tolerances, and validates the tool itself: false
alarms on correct code, margin between observed error and tolerance, accuracy of
the reference against 50-digit arithmetic, and an audit of the generators.
\end{itemize}
The library, the experiments and the data are available at
\url{https://github.com/clement-basdevant/dsp-props} under a BSD licence.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Background and related work}
\label{sec:related}
% ===========================================================================

\subsection{Testing without an oracle}
Metamorphic testing~\cite{chen2018metamorphic,segura2016metamorphic}, applied
among others to bioinformatics~\cite{chen2009bioinformatics} and image
processing~\cite{jafari2024image}, checks
\emph{metamorphic relations}: if $f$ is correct, then for related inputs $x$
and $x'$ the outputs $f(x)$ and $f(x')$ must satisfy a known relation, \eg
$f(x+x') = f(x)+f(x')$ for a linear $f$. Property-based testing (PBT), introduced
by QuickCheck~\cite{claessen2000quickcheck} and available in Python through
Hypothesis~\cite{maciver2019hypothesis}, generates the inputs and shrinks a
failing input to a minimal one~\cite{maciver2020reduction}. Both are general
techniques: the relations, the generators and the comparison rule are left to
the user. Interviews of PBT users identify writing properties and generators as
their main weakness~\cite{goldstein2024pbt}; Maaz
et~al.\ use language models to propose properties across the Python ecosystem~\cite{maaz2025agentic}.

\subsection{Self-testing of numerical programs}
Blum, Luby and Rubinfeld~\cite{blum1993selftesting} showed that a program
computing a linear function can be tested, and even corrected, by checking
random linear identities. Erg\"un~\cite{ergun1995testing,ergun2000selftesting}
extended the idea to multivariate linear functions such as the DFT, and
Erg\"un, Kumar and Rubinfeld~\cite{ergun2001checking} to computations that are
only approximately correct. The FFTW library~\cite{frigo2005fftw} ships a
self-test built on these results, which checks linearity, impulse responses and
time and frequency shifts~\cite{fftwverify}. These works establish that
linearity and shift identities characterise the DFT; they do not cover
filters, resamplers or streaming code, and they treat the floating-point error
with a single threshold.

\subsection{Differential testing and numerical faults}
Differential testing compares several implementations of the same
function~\cite{vanover2020fpdiff}. It needs at least two of them, and they may
share an algorithm or an assumption, \eg the same handling of an empty block.
Di Franco et~al.\ analysed 269 real numerical bugs in NumPy, SciPy, LAPACK,
GSL and Elemental~\cite{difranco2017floatingpoint}, showing that such bugs reach
widely used, mature libraries.

\subsection{Floating-point error of DSP operators}
The FFT computed by a Cooley--Tukey algorithm has a relative error that grows
as $O(\eps\log N)$~\cite{schatzman1996accuracy,higham2002accuracy}, where $\eps$
is the unit roundoff, whereas the direct DFT grows as $O(\eps N)$. The error of a
linear recursion depends on the conditioning of its poles~\cite{higham2002accuracy}.
These bounds are rarely used in tests, which fall back on fixed relative tolerances.

\subsection{Mutation analysis}
To compare test approaches, we inject faults with mutation
operators~\cite{offutt1996mutation,jia2011mutation,papadakis2019mutation}.
Detection of mutants correlates with detection of real
faults~\cite{just2014mutants}.

% ===========================================================================
\section{How DSP libraries test themselves}
\label{sec:survey}
% ===========================================================================

To make P1--P3 concrete, we analysed the syntax trees of the test suites of
\code{numpy.fft}, \code{scipy.fft}, \code{scipy.signal}, librosa~\cite{mcfee2015librosa}
and the functional module of torchaudio (script
\code{benchmarks/survey\_test\_suites.py}, results in
\code{survey\_results.json}). Table~\ref{tab:survey} summarises the counts. They
are syntactic heuristics: a comparison is counted when a known assertion
function is called, and its tolerance when a literal is passed as
\code{rtol}, \code{atol}, \code{decimal} or similar.

\input{tables/survey.tex}

No test uses Hypothesis or any other input generator. Hand-written tolerances
are frequent and heterogeneous, which reflects P3: each test author picks a
value that makes the test pass on their machine. Empty inputs appear in a few
tests, but the combination that exposed the \code{lfilter} and \code{sosfilt}
faults appears in \surveyZiEmpty{} tests only.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Contribution}
\label{sec:contrib}
% ===========================================================================

dsp-props is a layer on top of Hypothesis. The user declares \emph{what an
operator is}, and the library derives the relations, the generators and the
tolerance. For instance, \code{@dp.lti\_filter(transfer=(b, a))} declares a
causal linear time-invariant (LTI) filter with transfer function $B(z)/A(z)$;
\code{dp.verify} then runs every applicable relation on generated inputs and
returns a report with the smallest failing input found by shrinking.

\subsection{Relations (answer to P1)}
Table~\ref{tab:relations} lists the relations per operator class. Each one is a
consequence of the declaration and is proved in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}; we
state them on finite sequences of length $N$, as implementations compute them,
which matters for shifts and edges. The relations replace the oracle: no
expected output is needed, except for the optional transfer function, which the
user states once instead of typing expected arrays.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Relations checked for each operator class}
\label{tab:relations}
\centering\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.27\columnwidth}p{0.66\columnwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Declaration & Relations \\
\midrule
Transform (DFT, real DFT, generic linear) & linearity; circular shift theorem; Parseval's identity (scale declared); Hermitian symmetry and real DC/Nyquist bins of a real input; inversion; convolution theorem \\
LTI filter & linearity; time invariance (delay with zero state); causality; frequency response equal to the declared $B/A$; output bounded by a declared gain for every input bounded by 1 \\
Rational resampler $L/M$ & linearity; output length $\lceil NL/M\rceil$; delay of $M$ input samples gives a delay of $L$ output samples; DC gain; rejection of tones above the output Nyquist frequency \\
Streaming / stateful & any split of the input into blocks, including empty and one-sample blocks, gives the one-shot output \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Generators (answer to P2)}
Signals are drawn from seven families: impulses, constants, sinusoids at
arbitrary frequency (including off-grid ones), sinusoids near the Nyquist
frequency, pairs of tones less than one DFT bin apart, sparse signals and white
noise; amplitudes are drawn from $\{10^{-100},10^{-3},1,10^{3},10^{100}\}$.
Lengths are biased towards 1, 2, small primes, and $2^k-1$, $2^k$, $2^k+1$, and
block splits include empty and one-sample blocks. The families are ordered so
that shrinking converges to short impulses, which yields readable counterexamples.

\subsection{Tolerances (answer to P3)}
All comparisons use the $\ell_2$ norm of the error, scaled by the norm of a
reference quantity, and a model of the admissible error.

\emph{FFT.} For transforms, $\|\hat y-y\|_2 \le c\,\eps\,\max(\log_2N,1)\,\|y\|_2 + N\,\mathrm{tiny}$,
the form of the forward error bound of the radix-2 FFT~\cite[Thm.~24.2]{higham2002accuracy},
with a constant $c$ that covers the few chained transforms in a relation, and a
floor at the smallest normal number $\mathrm{tiny}$ that keeps exact zeros
strict while tolerating underflow.

\emph{Linear recursions.} For a filter $y=(B/A)x$ computed by a direct-form
recursion, Appendix~\ref{app:iir} derives
\begin{equation}
\|\hat y-y\|_2 \le c\,\eps\,k\,\|h_A\|_1\bigl(\|b\|_1+\|a_{1:}\|_1\|h_{B/A}\|_1\bigr)\|x\|_2,
\label{eq:iir}
\end{equation}
to first order in $\eps$, where $k$ is the number of coefficients, $h_A$ and
$h_{B/A}$ are the impulse responses of $1/A$ and $B/A$, and $a_{1:}$ are the
feedback coefficients. The bound grows as poles approach the unit circle, which
is where recursions lose accuracy.

\emph{Calibration.} An analytic bound cannot describe every library: an FFT
may switch algorithm with the factorisation of $N$. \code{dp.calibrate}
measures the error of an implementation against an extended-precision
reference for every length and turns it into a per-length tolerance. It refuses
to calibrate when the error exceeds what rounding can explain ($10^6\eps$), so a
fault cannot be absorbed into the tolerance.

\subsection{Differences with the state of the art}
Compared with generic PBT, dsp-props supplies the three pieces of domain
knowledge that PBT leaves to the user; Section~\ref{sec:rq2} measures the
contribution of two of them. Compared with self-testing of the
DFT~\cite{ergun1995testing,fftwverify}, it covers filters, resamplers and
streaming code, and its tolerance follows the operator. Compared with
differential testing~\cite{vanover2020fpdiff}, it needs a single implementation.
Compared with the test suites of Section~\ref{sec:survey}, it needs no expected
values and no hand-chosen tolerance.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
% ===========================================================================

We answer four research questions (RQ).
\textbf{RQ1}: does dsp-props detect more faults than the state of practice?
\textbf{RQ2}: what do the domain generators and the error-model tolerances contribute?
\textbf{RQ3}: is dsp-props itself correct, \ie free of false alarms, with sound references and generators?
\textbf{RQ4}: does it find faults in real libraries?

\paragraph*{Environment} \envDescription. All runs use
\code{max\_examples=200} per relation, the library default.

\subsection{RQ1 and RQ2: fault detection on generated mutants}
\label{sec:rq1}

\paragraph*{Subjects} We wrote four small reference implementations with the
interface of a library function (\code{benchmarks/comparison/subjects/}): a
radix-2 FFT with Bluestein's algorithm for other lengths, a direct-form~II
transposed \code{lfilter} with initial state, a polyphase \code{upfirdn} used by
a port of \code{resample\_poly}, and a block FIR filter by overlap-add. All four
agree with NumPy or SciPy to a relative error below $1.6\times10^{-15}$ and pass
every suite below.

\paragraph*{Faults} \code{mutate.py} generates every first-order mutant with
the classic operators~\cite{offutt1996mutation}: arithmetic, bitwise and
relational operator replacement, constant replacement ($k\to k\pm1$,
$c\to c+1$), unary minus deletion, \code{min}/\code{max} swap and statement
deletion, giving \nMutAuto{} mutants (\nMutFft{} FFT, \nMutLfilter{}
\code{lfilter}, \nMutUpfirdn{} \code{upfirdn}, \nMutOla{} overlap-add).

\paragraph*{Ground truth} An oracle used only for classification runs each
mutant on a fixed battery of inputs (all lengths up to 130 and several larger
ones for the FFT, many filters, including order 0, and initial states for \code{lfilter}, rates up
to $5/4$ and $1/7$ for \code{upfirdn} with and without default arguments,
random block splits for overlap-add) and
compares with an independent reference. A mutant is \emph{equivalent} if its
largest relative error is at most $10^{-12}$, an \emph{accuracy} fault if it is
between $10^{-12}$ and $10^{-6}$, and a \emph{functional} fault above $10^{-6}$,
or if it raises, returns the wrong shape or exceeds the time limit. This gives
\nFunctional{} functional faults and \nEquivalent{} equivalent mutants. No mutant
falls in the accuracy band: the largest relative error of a mutant is either below
$10^{-14}$ or above 1. First-order mutation of these subjects thus produces gross
faults only, and we study accuracy faults with the hand-written mutants below.

\paragraph*{Approaches} \emph{SoP} (state of practice) is the test suite of
the library whose interface the subject implements, ported test by test with
its inputs and tolerances: NumPy's and SciPy's FFT tests, SciPy's
\code{lfilter}, \code{lfilter\_zi}, \code{upfirdn} and \code{resample\_poly}
tests, including the regression test added for gh-22571; the overlap-add
subject, which has no library counterpart, gets four tests in the same style.
\emph{dsp-props} runs the declarations a user would write (two to four per
subject). Two ablations isolate the components: \emph{uniform} replaces the
domain generators by uniform lengths in $[1,512]$ and values in $[-1,1]$, and
\emph{fixed-tol} replaces every tolerance model by a fixed relative tolerance of
$10^{-7}$ (the default of \code{numpy.testing.assert\_allclose}); \emph{generic
PBT} applies both, \ie the same relations written with Hypothesis alone. Each
randomised approach runs with \nSeeds{} seeds; a run that exceeds
\timeoutSeconds{}~s counts as a detection, since a hanging test fails in
continuous integration.

\input{tables/comparison.tex}

\paragraph*{RQ1} Table~\ref{tab:comparison} gives the share of mutants
detected, averaged over seeds. \rqOneText

\paragraph*{Hand-written faults} The repository also contains \nMutHand{}
hand-written faults in six families, closer to real bugs (a forgotten $1/N$, a
twiddle sign error, single-precision intermediates, a filter that changes after
64 samples, a gain wrong by 1\,\%, a missing interpolation gain, state reset
between blocks; script \code{mutants/run\_mutants.py}). The four
single-precision faults are accuracy faults in the sense above. dsp-props detects \handKilled{} of them;
\handFirstThree{} fail within the first three generated inputs, and the median
length of the shrunk counterexample is \handMedianLen{} samples. One fault class
is a documented blind spot: a filter whose gain is wrong by 1\% is still linear,
time-invariant and causal, and is detected only when its transfer function is
declared.

\input{tables/hand.tex}

\paragraph*{RQ2}\label{sec:rq2} \rqTwoText

\subsection{RQ3: is the tool itself correct?}
\label{sec:rq3}

A reviewer of any fault-finding tool should ask whether its alarms are real.
We check four things (script \code{benchmarks/validation.py}, results in
\code{validation.json}).

\paragraph*{Relations} Every relation is a theorem about the declared class of
operators (Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}), so a correct implementation in exact
arithmetic never violates it; only the floating-point comparison can raise a
false alarm.

\paragraph*{False alarms} We ran every declaration on correct implementations,
NumPy's FFT and real FFT, SciPy's \code{lfilter}, \code{sosfilt},
\code{upfirdn} and \code{resample\_poly}, and the four reference subjects, with
\fpSeeds{} independent seeds: \fpRuns{} runs of a relation, \fpComparisons{}
floating-point comparisons, \fpFailed{} failures. SciPy's \code{lfilter} with
an initial state on empty blocks is excluded from this count because it is the
known fault gh-22571; dsp-props flags it in \knownBugFlagged{} of
\knownBugRuns{} runs on SciPy \scipyVersion.

\paragraph*{Margin} During the same runs we recorded the ratio of the observed
error to the tolerance for every comparison. \marginExact{} of the comparisons
are exact (ratio 0); the 99th percentile is \marginPnn{} and the maximum
\marginMax: the tolerance is \marginFactor{} times larger than the worst error
observed on correct code.
Table~\ref{tab:hand} shows that it is nevertheless tight enough to catch the
single-precision faults.

\paragraph*{References} Calibration and the tests of the IIR model compare
against extended-precision references, a DFT computed by NumPy in
\code{long double} and a direct recursion in \code{long double}. Against
a 50-digit computation with mpmath, their relative error is at most
\refDftMax{}$\,\eps$ and \refLfilterMax{}$\,\eps$ respectively, where $\eps$ is
the double-precision unit roundoff: the references are three orders of
magnitude more accurate than what they are used to measure.

\paragraph*{Generators} We sampled each generator and checked its claims.
All \genPathoCount{} pathological lengths are produced, impulses have
exactly one non-zero sample, all signals are finite and of the requested
length, and amplitudes cover $10^{-100}$ to $10^{100}$; \genEmptyBlock{} of
block splits contain an empty block and \genOneBlock{} a one-sample block;
near-Nyquist frequencies lie in $[0.45,0.5]$; \genCloseBelowOne{} of the tone
pairs are less than one bin apart. The audit also found a weakness: the
``off-grid'' sinusoid lands exactly on a DFT bin in \genOnGrid{} of draws,
because Hypothesis favours simple values such as 0 and $0.5$ (\genZeroNyq{} of
draws). These are useful edge cases, but the family is less often off-grid than
its name says; a future version will draw both on-grid and strictly off-grid
frequencies.

\subsection{RQ4: faults in real libraries}
\label{sec:rq4}
A campaign over \campaignTargets{} targets in SciPy, NumPy, PyTorch, librosa
and torchaudio (\code{benchmarks/campaign.py}) produced the following findings.
\begin{itemize}
\item \code{scipy.signal.lfilter} returns an uninitialised final state, and
\code{sosfilt} raises, when given an empty block with an initial state. The
\code{lfilter} part is an independent rediscovery of gh-22571, fixed in the
development version after SciPy~1.18.1; the \code{sosfilt} part, which fails on
any input that is empty along the filtered axis, was new. The same fault makes
librosa's streaming pre-emphasis fail on an empty block.
\item \code{scipy.signal.tf2sos} drops pure delays: for $y[n]=x[n-2]$ it
returns an identity section, so \code{sosfilt(tf2sos(b, a), x)} differs from
\code{lfilter(b, a, x)}.
\item torchaudio's \code{deemphasis}, documented as the inverse of
\code{preemphasis}, clamps its output to $[-1,1]$.
\item PyTorch's CPU FFT reaches \torchMaxEps$\,\eps$ for $N=\torchWorstN$, against at most
\numpyMaxEps$\,\eps$ for NumPy over $N=2,\dots,1200$
(Fig.~\ref{fig:profile}); this is not a fault, but it shows why one fixed
tolerance cannot fit every library.
\end{itemize}
The campaign also produced \campaignTriaged{} alarms that triage traced to
errors in our own specifications (\eg \code{filtfilt} is not symmetric under time
reversal with its default padding); they are listed in the repository.

\subsection{Threats to validity}
Mutants are a proxy for real faults~\cite{just2014mutants}; the hand-written
faults and the bugs of RQ4 complement them. The SoP suites are ports of real
suites restricted to the subject's interface; the original suites also test
other dtypes and shapes. The subjects are small, and the oracle thresholds
($10^{-12}$, $10^{-6}$) are a choice; per-mutant errors are in the result file
so that other thresholds can be applied. The oracle was extended once after the
first run: it did not call \code{upfirdn} with its default arguments nor
\code{lfilter} with an order-0 filter, so it labelled as equivalent eight mutants
that the SoP suites or dsp-props detected; with the extended oracle, no approach
detects any equivalent mutant. The kill rates of dsp-props depend on the
declarations, which we wrote before running the mutants and did not change
afterwards. Results depend on random seeds, which we vary and report.

\paragraph*{Reproducing} The scripts \code{run\_comparison.py} and
\code{run\_hand\_mutants.py} (in \code{benchmarks/comparison/}),
\code{benchmarks/validation.py}, \code{mutants/run\_mutants.py} and
\code{benchmarks/survey\_test\_suites.py} produce the result files, and
\code{paper/article/make\_numbers.py} turns them into every number and table of
this article.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% ===========================================================================
DSP code is tested against expected values that someone computed elsewhere,
with tolerances chosen case by case, on inputs that rarely include the cases
that break it. Generic property-based and metamorphic testing remove the need for
expected values but leave the relations, the inputs and the tolerances to each
developer. dsp-props supplies these three pieces for transforms, filters,
resamplers and streaming code. \conclusionResult{} It raised no false alarm on
correct implementations, its references and generators were audited, and the
audit itself revealed a weakness that we report.

We reported the faults found to the projects concerned: the empty-block fault of
\code{lfilter} and \code{sosfilt} to SciPy (issue \#26406, the \code{lfilter} part
being a duplicate of gh-22571), with a proposed fix (pull request \#26415),
\reportedOthers

\section{Proofs of the relations}
\label{app:proofs}
% ===========================================================================

Sequences have length $N$, indices are taken modulo $N$ for the DFT, and
$\DFT x[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]\,\omega^{kn}$ with $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/N}$.

\begin{proposition}[Linearity] $\DFT$ is linear, and so is every LTI filter
from zero state and every resampler of the form ``upsample by $L$, filter,
downsample by $M$''.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} Each is a composition of linear maps: a matrix product for
$\DFT$; zero insertion, convolution with $h$ and decimation for the resampler; for
a filter from zero state, $y$ is the convolution $h*x$ truncated to $N$ samples.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Circular shift] If $x_s[n]=x[n-s]$, then $\DFT x_s[k]=\omega^{ks}\DFT x[k]$.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} $\sum_n x[n-s]\omega^{kn}=\sum_m x[m]\omega^{k(m+s)}$ with $m=n-s$
running over all residues.\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Parseval] $\|\DFT x\|_2^2=N\|x\|_2^2$.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} $\DFT=\sqrt N\,U$ with $U$ unitary, since
$\sum_k\omega^{k(n-m)}=N\delta_{nm}$.\end{proof}
A transform declared with another normalisation states its scale, which is
checked instead of $N$.

\begin{proposition}[Hermitian symmetry] If $x$ is real, $\DFT x[N-k]=\overline{\DFT x[k]}$;
in particular $\DFT x[0]$ and, for even $N$, $\DFT x[N/2]$ are real.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} $\omega^{(N-k)n}=\overline{\omega^{kn}}$ and $x$ is real. For
$k=0$ and $k=N/2$, the bin is its own conjugate.\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Inversion and convolution] $\DFT^{-1}\DFT x=x$, and
$\DFT^{-1}(\DFT x\cdot\DFT y)=x\circledast y$, the circular convolution.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} The first follows from $\DFT^{-1}=\frac1N\overline{\DFT}$ and
Parseval's orthogonality. For the second, $\DFT(x\circledast y)[k]
=\sum_n\sum_m x[m]y[n-m]\omega^{kn}=\DFT x[k]\,\DFT y[k]$ by the shift
proposition.\end{proof}
dsp-props computes $x\circledast y$ directly in $O(N^2)$, independently of
the operator under test.

\begin{proposition}[Time invariance and causality on finite sequences] Let
$f$ be a causal LTI filter applied from zero state, $f(x)[n]=\sum_{m\le n}h[n-m]x[m]$.
Then (i) $f([0_s,x])=[0_s,f(x)]$ on $N+s$ samples, and (ii) if $x$ and $x'$
agree on $[0,k)$, then $f(x)$ and $f(x')$ agree on $[0,k)$.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} (i) For $n<s$ the sum only involves zeros; for $n\ge s$,
substitute $m'=m-s$. (ii) $f(x)[n]$ for $n<k$ only involves $x[m]$, $m\le n<k$.
\end{proof}
For a non-causal filter (\eg a centred FIR), (i) holds after discarding the
first $s$ output samples, which is what the library checks.

\begin{proposition}[Transfer function] For a stable causal filter with
transfer function $H=B/A$ and impulse response $h$, the length-$L$ DFT of
$(h[0],\dots,h[L-1])$ equals $H(e^{2\pi i k/L})$ up to the aliasing term
$\sum_{n\ge L}h[n]\omega_L^{kn}$, whose norm is bounded by $\sum_{n\ge L}|h[n]|$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} $H(e^{i\theta})=\sum_{n\ge0}h[n]e^{-i\theta n}$ converges
absolutely for a stable filter; split the sum at $L$.\end{proof}
The library chooses $L$ so that $r^L<10^{-17}$, with $r$ the largest pole
modulus, and adds the tail to the tolerance.

\begin{proposition}[Bounded gain] For an LTI filter with $\|h\|_1\le G$,
every input with $|x[n]|\le1$ gives $|y[n]|\le G$, and the input
$x[m]=\mathrm{sign}(h[N-1-m])$ attains $\sum_{n<N}|h[n]|$ at $n=N-1$.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} $|y[n]|\le\sum_m|h[n-m]||x[m]|\le\|h\|_1$; with the given input,
every term of $y[N-1]=\sum_m h[N-1-m]x[m]$ is $|h[N-1-m]|$.\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Periodic time invariance] Let
$f=\downarrow_M\circ(h*\cdot)\circ\uparrow_L$. Delaying the input by $Ms$
samples delays the output by $Ls$ samples.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} $\uparrow_L$ turns a delay of $Ms$ into a delay of $LMs$; the
filter preserves it; $\downarrow_M$ turns a delay of $LMs$, a multiple of $M$,
into a delay of $Ls$.\end{proof}
The output length $\lceil NL/M\rceil$, the DC gain and the alias rejection are
declared specifications rather than theorems; their tolerances (ripple,
stop-band level) are part of the declaration.

\begin{proposition}[Block invariance] Let a streaming processor be a state
machine $(q_{t+1},y_t)=\phi(q_t,x_t)$ applied sample by sample, and let
\code{process} on a block apply $\phi$ to its samples in order, starting from the
current state and storing the final one. Then for any split
$x=x^{(1)}\cdots x^{(J)}$, including empty blocks,
$\mathrm{concat}_j\,\code{process}(x^{(j)})=\code{process}(x)$ from the same
initial state.\end{proposition}
\begin{proof} By induction on $J$: an empty block leaves the state unchanged and
outputs nothing, and processing $x^{(1)}$ then $x^{(2)}$ applies $\phi$ to the
samples of $x^{(1)}x^{(2)}$ in order.\end{proof}
Block-based algorithms such as overlap-add are not sample-by-sample machines,
but a correct one computes the same function, which is what the relation checks.

\section{Error bound of a linear recursion}
\label{app:iir}
% ===========================================================================
Normalise $a_0=1$. The direct recursion computes
$y[n]=\sum_{j=0}^{q}b_jx[n-j]-\sum_{j=1}^{p}a_jy[n-j]$ with $k=p+q+1$ products.
In floating point, with the standard model~\cite{higham2002accuracy}, the
computed $\hat y$ satisfies
$\hat y[n]=\sum_jb_jx[n-j]-\sum_ja_j\hat y[n-j]+\delta[n]$ with
$|\delta[n]|\le\gamma_k\bigl(\sum_j|b_j||x[n-j]|+\sum_j|a_j||\hat y[n-j]|\bigr)$,
$\gamma_k=k\eps/(1-k\eps)$. The error $e=\hat y-y$ therefore obeys
$A(z)e=\delta$, \ie $e=h_A*\delta$. By Young's inequality
$\|e\|_2\le\|h_A\|_1\|\delta\|_2$, and
$\|\delta\|_2\le\gamma_k(\|b\|_1\|x\|_2+\|a_{1:}\|_1\|\hat y\|_2)$. Finally
$\|\hat y\|_2\le\|h_{B/A}\|_1\|x\|_2+\|e\|_2$, which gives
\eqref{eq:iir} to first order in $\eps$, with $\gamma_k\approx k\eps$. The library
uses $c=4$ to cover the two computations compared in a relation, and the
validation of Section~\ref{sec:rq3} confirms that the bound is never reached on
correct code.
